Their lower heat of hydration helps control early thermal cracking in a thick raft.

questions.q: 'The most effective thing civil engineers can do to reach net zero is to build less, not to build better.' Discuss this proposition with reference to whole life carbon, the PAS 2080 approach and the need for resilient infrastructure in the UK.
markScheme: Defines whole life carbon (EN 15978 modules A–D), embodied vs operational, and why embodied carbon dominates many infrastructure assets
Explains the PAS 2080 hierarchy (avoid, switch, improve in the 2023 edition; build nothing, build less, build clever, build efficiently in 2016) and that savings are largest at early stages
Supports the proposition: avoiding or reusing assets removes carbon entirely, while material substitution yields percentage savings; examples such as retrofitting rather than replacing
Uses quantitative reasoning (e.g. cement roughly 8% of global CO₂; GGBS might save around a quarter of concrete carbon, but avoiding the element saves all of it)
Challenges: some infrastructure enables large operational reductions (rail electrification, renewable grid connections, active travel), so 'building' can cut whole-system carbon
Resilience: climate adaptation (flood defences, drainage, heat resilience) requires new or upgraded assets; under-provision risks failures and reconstruction carbon
Better building matters: lean design, low-carbon materials, durability and long design life reduce whole-life carbon; maintenance and replacement (B-modules)
System boundaries and rebound effects: capacity expansion may induce demand; carbon accounting must be consistent
Legal and policy context: Climate Change Act 2008 (net zero 2050), Planning Act 2008 decision-making, the role of clients and the value chain
Reasoned conclusion: the hierarchy suggests 'build less' first, but the real aim is minimum whole-life, whole-system carbon while meeting needs and resilience, so it is a false dichotomy
questions.modelAnswer:
The proposition draws on a central insight of carbon management, though it oversimplifies. Whole life carbon, as structured by BS EN 15978, covers product and construction (A1–A5), use, including maintenance, replacement and operational energy (B1–B7), end of life (C1–C4) and benefits beyond the boundary (D). For roads, bridges and pipelines, embodied carbon in materials and construction often dominates, because operational energy is small. Concrete and steel are the major contributors, and cement alone accounts for roughly 8% of global CO₂ (Chatham House, 2018).

PAS 2080:2023 supports 'build less' directly. Its hierarchy puts avoid (in the 2016 wording, build nothing and build less) above switch and improve (build clever and build efficiently), because avoiding an asset removes all its carbon, while substitution only trims a percentage. Replacing CEM I with GGBS might save about a quarter of a raft's concrete carbon. Retaining and strengthening an existing structure can avoid most of it. The ability to influence carbon also falls as design advances, which favours early, scope-level challenge.

Yet 'build less' cannot be absolute. Some infrastructure enables reductions elsewhere. Electrified rail, grid reinforcement for renewables and active-travel networks carry embodied carbon but cut operational emissions across the economy, so the right test is whole-system carbon. Resilience pulls the same way. Climate change raises flood and heat risks, and inadequate drainage or defences lead to failures, disruption and carbon-intensive reconstruction. Under-building can increase lifetime emissions.

'Building better' therefore remains essential. Lean structural design, low-carbon materials, durability and long service lives reduce A and B module emissions and avoid premature replacement. Consistent system boundaries, and attention to induced demand from capacity schemes, stop carbon accounting from being gamed.

In conclusion, the hierarchy rightly puts questioning need first. The Climate Change Act's net zero target is best served by building only what is needed, and building it well. Treating 'less' and 'better' as rivals is a false choice.
